title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer: Nathan Fielder’s Shocking Documentary with Elizabeth Holmes Exposed
body:
The latest trailer for “You Can See Everything,” the documentary that follows comedian‑turned‑filmmaker Nathan Fielder’s uneasy partnership with disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has been released by A24, igniting fresh buzz ahead of the awards season. The 15‑minute preview offers a tantalizing glimpse of the film’s blend of investigative journalism, dark humor, and intimate confrontation, showing Fielder sharing a cramped Airbnb with Holmes, coaxing an emotional outburst, and later grilling her husband, former Theranos chief engineer Sunny Balwani, in a stark interrogation room. The trailer’s stark visual language and unsettling tone suggest a project that could redefine the documentary form while cementing Fielder’s reputation as a provocateur who blurs the line between comedy and real‑world consequence.

The documentary, directed by Fielder and co‑director Lance Oppenheim, has been shrouded in secrecy since its announcement earlier this year. Its title, “You Can See Everything,” references a phrase Holmes reportedly used during the 2022 trial, hinting at the film’s focus on transparency—or the illusion of it. The trailer confirms that the narrative will weave together footage from the 2021 trial, private conversations captured in Holmes’s home, and newly recorded interviews with former Theranos employees. By juxtaposing courtroom drama with off‑camera moments, the filmmakers appear intent on exposing the human cost of the biotech fraud beyond the headline‑grabbing headlines.

Fielder’s involvement is a point of intrigue for both critics and fans. Best known for “Nathan For You,” where he used absurd business ideas to satirize corporate culture, he has previously flirted with documentary territory in the mock‑reality series “The Rehearsal.” Here, however, the stakes feel higher. The trailer shows him adopting a quasi‑journalistic posture—camera in hand, notebook open—while also employing his signature deadpan humor to disarm his subjects. Observers note that this hybrid approach could challenge traditional documentary ethics, raising questions about consent, manipulation, and the role of a filmmaker who is simultaneously a performer and an investigator.

The film also arrives at a moment when the public’s appetite for true‑crime and corporate scandal narratives is at a peak. Recent documentaries such as “The Tinder Swindler” and “The Great Hack” have demonstrated that audiences are eager for stories that combine investigative depth with cinematic flair. “You Can See Everything” seems poised to tap into that demand, but it also risks re‑opening wounds for those still grappling with the fallout of Theranos’s collapse. The trailer’s depiction of Holmes breaking down in tears—an emotionally charged moment that feels both raw and orchestrated—has sparked debate on whether the documentary will humanize a figure many view as a cautionary tale or inadvertently provide her a platform for redemption.

Industry insiders predict that the film could become a strong contender in the documentary categories at the upcoming Oscars and Golden Globes, especially given A24’s track record of championing auteur‑driven nonfiction projects. The studio’s involvement adds a layer of prestige and distribution muscle that could propel the film beyond the festival circuit into mainstream theaters. Moreover, the collaboration between a comedy veteran and a documentary specialist may inspire a new wave of genre‑blending projects, encouraging other creators to experiment with narrative structures that defy conventional categorization.

As the release date approaches, anticipation builds not only around the film’s artistic merits but also around its potential impact on the broader conversation about corporate accountability and media responsibility. Whether “You Can See Everything” will deliver a definitive portrait of Elizabeth Holmes or simply add another chapter to the Theranos saga remains to be seen. One thing is clear: the trailer has set the stage for a compelling, unsettling exploration of truth, deception, and the uneasy dance between humor and horror—a combination that could resonate long after the credits roll.
